# 1 Samuel Chapter 21 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 163 | **Source Images:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/1SA_021_page_001.jpg, 1SA_021_page_002.jpg

---

**1** And David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came trembling to meet David, and he said to him, "Why are you alone, and no one is with you?"

**2** And David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I am sending you, and with which I have charged you.' And the young men I have directed to such and such a place.

**3** Now then, what is under your hand? Give me five loaves of bread in my hand, or whatever may be found."

**4** And the priest answered David and said, "There is no common bread under my hand, but there is holy bread — if only the young men have kept themselves from women."

**5** And David answered the priest and said to him, "Surely women have been kept from us as in times past when I went out, and the vessels of the young men are holy. And it is an ordinary journey — how much more so today will it be holy in their vessels."

**6** So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD, in order to put hot bread in its place on the day it was taken away.

**7** Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. And his name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of the herdsmen who belonged to Saul.

**8** And David said to Ahimelech, "Is there not here under your hand a spear or a sword? For I brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's matter was urgent."

**9** And the priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah — behold, it is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you wish to take that, take it, for there is no other except that one here." And David said, "There is none like it; give it to me."

**10** And David arose and fled that day from before Saul. And he came to Achish king of Gath.

**11** And the servants of Achish said to him, "Is this not David, the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in the dances, saying: 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"

**12** And David took these words to his heart and was very much afraid before Achish king of Gath.

**13** And he changed his behavior before their eyes and feigned madness in their hands. And he scratched marks on the doors of the gate and let his saliva run down upon his beard.

**14** And Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see the man is mad. Why do you bring him to me?

**15** Am I lacking madmen, that you have brought this one to rave in my presence? Shall this one come into my house?"

**16** And David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all the house of his father heard of it, they went down to him there.

---

## LOGOS Translation Notes

Chapter 21 presents David's flight from Saul through two episodes: his deception at Nob and his feigned madness at Gath. The Hebrew versification in the Leningrad Codex differs from English Bibles by one verse (the MT begins this chapter at 20:42b in some traditions); this translation follows the standard English versification of 16 verses.

Key lexical decisions: In verse 5, the phrase כְּלֵי הַנְּעָרִים (kley hanne'arim) is rendered "vessels of the young men," preserving the Hebrew metaphor. In verse 7, נֶעְצָר (ne'etsar) is rendered "detained" — the precise sense of his being held at the sanctuary remains debated. The verb וַיְשַׁנֹּא (vayyeshannoh) in verse 13 follows the reading "he changed" (from שׁנה), referring to David's alteration of his rational behavior. The term וַיְתַהֹלֵל (vayyithholel) denotes feigning madness, from the root הלל in the Hithpael.

Doeg the Edomite (v. 7) is introduced with ominous brevity — his being "detained before the LORD" may indicate a vow or ritual obligation, but the narrator's purpose is to place a witness at the scene whose testimony will prove fatal in chapter 22.

— LOGOS (Λόγος), translated from the Leningrad Codex (B19A)
